slides.title: Classification
slides.content: Classification • Classification = automatically assigning an instance to one of a predefined set of categories • Widely used in NLP: • Document/topic classification (e.g. sports, politics, culture) • Sentiment analysis (positive, negative, neutral) • Part-of-speech tagging (noun, verb, adjective, …) • Named entity recognition (person, location, organization, …) • Often a binary task (yes/no, true/false), but can also be multi-class or multi-label 2/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Rule-based
slides.content: Rule-based 1 IF exists word in document such that word in ['exciting', 'entertaining', ...] THEN output POSITIVE 2 IF exists word in document such that word in ['hated', 'worst', ...] THEN output NEGATIVE • Easy to interpret and adjust • But: labor-intensive and not generalizable 3/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Machine learning
slides.content: Machine learning supervised and non-supervised • Supervised learning • Train a system on a classification task • We need a training set: a set of manually labeled instances • We equally define important characteristics: features • A machine learning algorithm allows us to associate features with labels • Performance is measured on a separate test set • Unsupervised learning • We induce object representations automatically, in order to generalize without manual intervention 6/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Supervised learning: feature-based learning
slides.content: Supervised learning: feature-based learning • Supervised learning is based on the concept of features (descriptors, characteristics) • Elementary indices, that link certain aspects of the observed data (d) to the class that we want to predict (c) • The prediction of the class c depends exclusively on the features f, constructed on the basis of the data d • Each feature has a numerical/categorical/boolean value • We apply machine learning algorithms on the basis of these features 7/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Feature model
slides.content: Feature model Examples • Text categorization • Class c: ‘medical’ • Data d: document • Features f: words (boolean/word count) • Author identification • Class c: ‘Charles Dickens’ • Data d: document (book) • Features f: extracted n-grams • Sentiment classification • Class c: ‘negative sentiment’ • Data d: tweet • Features f: words 8/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Feature-based model
slides.content: Feature-based model Linear classifier • Classification from a set of features {fi} to a number of classes {c} • Attribute a weight λi,c for each feature fi and each class c • For a certain pair (c, d), the features will vote with their weights • We pick the class c that maximizes the sum of the various features • Different ways for choosing the weights (optimization) 9/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Feature-based model
slides.content: Feature-based model Linear classifier: example • Text classification • As features, we take the frequency of lemmas • maxc∈C ! i λi,cfi “The virus predominantly targets Windows computers.” λi,j class cj feature fi computer science biology virus 0.5 0.6 target 0.4 0.2 computer 0.8 -0.6 Windows 0.9 -1.2 • vote(computer science) = 0.5 × 1 + 0.4 × 1 + 0.8 × 1 + 0.9 × 1 = 2.6 • vote(biology) = 0.6 × 1 + 0.2 × 1 + (−0.6) × 1 + (−1.2) × 1 = −1.0 10/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Feature-based model
slides.content: Feature-based model Logistic regression • Linear scores (range −∞to ∞) are difficult to interpret, we’d like to have probabilities • We construct a probabilistic model on the basis of the linear model • Transform the values to probabilities using the exponential function + normalization • We choose the parameters λc,i that maximize the likelihood based on the training data P(c | d, λ) = exp(! i λc,ifi) ! c′∈C exp(! i λc′,ifi) • P(computer science | d) = e2.6/(e2.6 + e−1.0) = 0.97 • P(biology | d) = e−1.0/(e2.6 + e−1.0) = 0.03 11/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Bayes’ theorem for sentiment classification
slides.content: Bayes’ theorem for sentiment classification cMAP = argmax c∈C P(c | d) = argmax c∈C P(d | c)P(c) P(d) ≃argmax c∈C P(d | c)P(c) ≃argmax c∈C P(x1, x2, . . . , xn | c)P(c) 23/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Bayes’ theorem for sentiment classification
slides.content: Bayes’ theorem for sentiment classification cMAP = argmax c∈C P(x1, x2, . . . , xn | c)P(c) • What is the probability of a class given that all features appear together in a document • Impossible to estimate this probability, unless we have a gigantic training set 24/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Independence hypotheses
slides.content: Independence hypotheses • Bag of words hypothesis: hypothesis that the order of words is not important • Conditional independence hypothesis: hypothesis that the probability of features (given the class) is independent • P(x1, x2, . . . , xn | c) = P(x1 | c) · P(x2 | c) · . . . · P(xn | c) 25/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Naive Bayes classifier
slides.content: Naive Bayes classifier cMAP = argmax c∈C P(x1, x2, . . . , xn | c)P(c) cNB = argmax c∈C P(c) " xi∈X P(xi | c) 26/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Train a naive Bayes classifier
slides.content: Train a naive Bayes classifier • First try: estimate maximum likelihood • We use the frequencies of the data P(cj) = doccount(C = cj) Ndoc P(wi | cj) = count(wi, cj) ! w∈V count(w, cj) 27/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Train a naive Bayes classifier
slides.content: Train a naive Bayes classifier P(wi | cj) = count(wi, cj) ! w∈V count(w, cj) • Fraction of time we see word wi out of all the words in the documents with class cj • How to estimate this quantity efficiently? • We create a large meta-document for a class j by concatenating all the documents of the same class • We use the frequency of w in this document 28/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Problem with maximum likelihood estimation
slides.content: Problem with maximum likelihood estimation • What happens when we don’t have any training documents with the word fantastic, labeled with the class positive ? P(fantastic | positive) = count(fantastic, positive) ! w∈V count(w, positive) = 0 • Problem: if a single probability in our product is zero, the entire probability is zero (even if we have other good evidence) • Zeros have a destructive influence cNB = argmax c∈C P(c) " xi∈X P(xi | c) 29/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Laplace smoothing (add-1) for naive Bayes classification
slides.content: Laplace smoothing (add-1) for naive Bayes classification P(wi | cj) = count(wi, cj) + 1 ! w∈V(count(w, cj) + 1) = count(wi, cj) + 1 (! w∈V count(w, cj)) + |V| 30/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Naive bayes classifier: algorithm
slides.content: Naive bayes classifier: algorithm 1 Extract the vocabulary V from our training corpus 2 Compute the probabilities P(cj) • for each class cj in C do • docsj ←all docs with class = cj • P(cj) ← |docsj| |#documents| 3 Compute the probabilities P(wi | cj) • textj ←concatenation of all docsj • for each word wi in V do • ni ←# occurrences of wi in textj • P(wi | cj) ← ni+1 n+|V| 31/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Other classifiers for sentiment classification
slides.content: Other classifiers for sentiment classification • Naive bayes is not the only possibility • Other approaches: • Logistic regression • Support vector machines (SVM) • Neural networks • Good implementations of various classifiers already exist; one just needs to define the features, and provide the training data 32/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Global optimization
slides.content: Global optimization • Problem: we perform a series of local judgements, without taking into account the global optimality • We hope that the local conditions give us a global optimum • To solve our problem: • Instead of emitting a single answer, predict the n best answers • This way, we can compute the best global sequence 40/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.content: Experiment • We have three sentiment classifiers • a list of hand-written rules (symbolic) • naive Bayes (statistical) • logistic regression (statistical) • Which one is better? how can we find out? • Common procedure in NLP: experiment 41/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Train, development, test
slides.content: Train, development, test training set dev test fit the model make choices report once • A model must be evaluated on data it has never seen: we care about generalization, not memorization • Training set: estimate the parameters (probabilities, weights) • Development (validation) set: for every choice you make (features, smoothing, thresholds, which model to keep: hyperparameters) • Test set: touched once, at the very end, for the number you report • Typical splits: 80/10/10 (train/dev/test) • Little data? Cross-validation on the training part; the test set still stays apart 42/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Leakage
slides.content: Leakage • Leakage: information about the test set finds its way into the model, so the reported score is too optimistic • It rarely looks like cheating: • you tried ten settings and kept the one that was best on the test set • the vocabulary was computed on all the data, before splitting • the same review (or a near-duplicate) occurs in both training and test • texts by the same author are included in both training and test • Everything that is learned or chosen must be learned or chosen without looking at the test set 43/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Baseline
slides.content: Baseline • ‘Our model reaches 95% accuracy’: is that good? • Example: toxic comment detection • about 95% of the comments are not toxic • A model that always answers not toxic scores 95%, while it does not find a single toxic comment • A number only means something next to a baseline • majority class (always predict the most frequent label) • a handful of simple rules, a word list • the simplest model that could possibly work • If your sophisticated model does not beat the simple baseline, you have a negative result 44/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Upper bound
slides.content: Upper bound • Opposite of the baseline: the best score that can be expected • Usually human performance: inter-annotator agreement • two annotators label the same items independently • percentage of agreement, or agreement corrected for chance (e.g. Krippendorff’s α) • The gold standard is only as reliable as the agreement between annotators • e.g. sentiment analysis: annotators often agree on 80–90% of the items • subjective tasks (irony, toxicity): considerably lower • A score is interpreted between baseline and upper bound 45/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Beyond accuracy
slides.content: Beyond accuracy Confusion matrix gold standard toxic not toxic system toxic true positive (TP) false positive (FP) not toxic false negative (FN) true negative (TN) P = TP TP + FP R = TP TP + FN F1 = 2PR P + R • The always-not toxic baseline: accuracy 95%, but recall and F1 for the class toxic: 0% 46/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Multiple classes
slides.content: Multiple classes • With more than two classes: compute P, R, F1 per class, then average • micro-average: pool all decisions →dominated by the frequent classes • macro-average: mean of the per-class scores →every class counts equally • With imbalanced classes, both averages can differ considerably 47/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Performance on sequences
slides.content: Performance on sequences • How to evaluate named entity recognition? • Precision, recall and F-measure, computed over entities rather than words • precision: percentage of entities returned by the system that are correct • recall: percentage of the entities in the test set that are found by the system • An entity is correct if both its boundaries and its type correspond to the test set • Charles Michel as PER, but only Michel tagged: incorrect • European Council tagged as LOC: incorrect • Per-word accuracy would be misleadingly high, as most words are labeled O 48/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Thresholds
slides.content: Thresholds • Naive Bayes and logistic regression output a probability • A decision requires a threshold, e.g. toxic if p > 0.5 • lower threshold: higher recall, lower precision • higher threshold: higher precision, lower recall • The threshold is a hyperparameter: it is set on the development set recall precision p > 0.9 p > 0.5 p > 0.1 49/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Significance
slides.content: Significance • Example: naive Bayes 84.2% accuracy, logistic regression 84.7% accuracy • Is logistic regression better? Not necessarily • the test set is a sample: a different set of 1,000 reviews yields a different score • models with random components (initialization, order of the data) yield different results with different random seeds • Guidelines: • use a sufficiently large test set; report size • repeat with different seeds or folds; report mean and standard deviation • small differences between models are often not significant: use a significance test (e.g. McNemar’s test, paired bootstrap) 50/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Error analysis
slides.content: Error analysis • An evaluation score indicates how often a model makes mistakes, not why • Error analysis: inspection of the errors on the development set • take a sample of errors (e.g. 50) and categorize them • which categories are frequent, and which could be addressed? • Linguistic knowledge is often helpful • Goal: explain a pattern of errors 51/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Checklist
slides.content: Checklist 1 Keep a separate test set, and use it only once 2 Avoid leakage 3 Compare against a baseline 4 Choose metrics that suit the task and the class distribution 5 Make all choices (incl. thresholds) on the development set 6 Report the uncertainty of the results 7 Analyze the errors 8 Support every claim with results 52/52 — Computational Linguistics — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be
